Former defense attorney here. Fucking THANK YOU for talking about Kelly Seigler’s shady ass.  Attorneys in that US have to take an oath to uphold the Constitution, but prosecutors are also sworn to uphold justice.  Their role isn’t just about convicting someone for a crime, it’s about making sure the RIGHT person is convicted… and Kelly Seigler is a prime example of how NOT to do the job. She doesn’t give a shit about victims or justice, she just wants to make herself look good.  And the fact that she was given a TV show despite her history of unethical conduct just makes me wanna vomit.

And for what it’s worth, Brady violations aren’t just corruption…it’s a very specific type of prosecutorial malfeasance.  Brady v. Maryland requires prosecutors to turn over any evidence to the defense that could be favorable to their case.  While accidentally or unintentionally failing to turn over information is technically a Brady violation, the letter shown on screen indicates that Siegler is alleged to have intentionally withheld information from the defense and then lied about it while under oath.  This is absolutely cause for disbarment and I really don’t know how the hell she still has a law license because this definitely isn’t the only time she’s been accused of this.  

Side note: I love ya, Mike. Your presentation style, sense of humor, and ability to discuss sensitive topics in a straightforward and unbiased way without losing sight of anyone’s humanity make you hands-down the best true crime creator on the interwebz.  Thank you for doing what you do!

comments.text: It’s so crazy how familiar this whole story seems to me. I know a guy who was accused of the murder of his high school girlfriend, but not actually charged until a decade later…and his case was also entirely circumstantial, and even more flimsy than this case. I didn’t know the victim, and didn’t meet the suspect until a couple years after the murder…tho I definitely knew about the case. A high school girl from a nearby small town went missing, and her body was discovered 2 weeks later. It was clear she’d been murdered…but to this day, no one knows how. The medical examiner’s could never agree on that. Of course her boyfriend was a suspect. They’d been known to argue a bit, and they were both mildly involved with drugs and alcohol (but so were all of their friends). No physical evidence was found. The only evidence was the testimony of several people who were trying to recall vague conversations from a decade earlier…and most of these witnesses admittedly used drugs and alcohol at the time. And not a single one stated that he’d confessed to the crime. A few claimed he’d made statements that they interpreted as an implication that he’d been involved…but that’s it. That was literally the entire case. Here’s what I know, personally. I met the suspect approximately 2 years after the murder, because he was in a relationship with my best friend’s sister. He’d been dating her since several months after the murder. I know that her parents were not thrilled about it…but after a few years, he became a part of their family. I didn’t know him well. I only really interacted with him a few times…but it was enough to allow me to form an opinion regarding his character. The first time we met was at my 21st birthday party. Everyone was drunk…many of us were smoking weed (including him and his girlfriend). He was very friendly and seemed genuinely kind…despite being somewhat intoxicated. He didn’t get very intoxicated at all…because he simply didn’t really want to. He liked to enjoy himself…but never to a point that it was problematic. He treated his girlfriend very well over the decade that I knew him…at least based on what I saw, and what I heard from people who were around them almost daily. The last time I saw him was shortly before he was arrested (10 years after the murder). I ran into him and his then wife (still the same girl he’d been with for a decade) at a bar, and they were both noticeably (but not sloppily) drunk. They even got into an argument, and I spoke to him about it outside. I don’t remember what the argument was about. I  do know that he was frustrated and upset…he even shed a few tears…but he wasn’t freaking out. He wasn’t angry. In no way did he seem like someone who could have become so angry that he’d lash out violently…even while intoxicated. A few months later, he was officially charged with murder, and was ultimately found guilty of manslaughter, and sentenced to 10 years in prison…less than a year after his first child was born. The trial was absurd in my opinion. Not even the slightest bit of physical evidence, or even an alleged confession. His character and his actions since the murder only suggested that he was a really decent guy. I don’t believe ANY case should be tried solely on circumstantial evidence…but I also can’t claim I know him to be innocent, for that same reason. He didn’t seem like a killer to me, or even someone who made a mistake and lied about it. That doesn’t, however, prove his innocence. Eventually, he received help from an organization that investigated cases of wrongful convictions, and they DID dig up some physical evidence. It wasn’t much…but it was the ONLY physical evidence in the case…and it was evidence not presented in his trial, because it was evidence discovered by a crime lab that never shared it with investigators. They didn’t share it, because they didn’t think it was significant. It was a drop of blood on the victims shoe…and it didn’t belong to the victim OR the man convicted of killing her. Had it been presented at trial, it would’ve been the only physical evidence on record…and it was evidence that could’ve exonerated him. When this came to light, his conviction was overturned, and he was released from prison 9 1/2 years into his 10-year sentence. It was only then that a major tv show (20/20) covered the case…and they, too, saw the injustice in it. Personally, I think it’s likely that Nichole is guilty…but I wouldn’t have found her guilty in a circumstantial case, either. She got lucky. The circumstantial evidence in her case was fairly damning, I think…but it still doesn’t prove anything beyond a reasonable doubt. Circumstantial evidence should only ever be used to strengthen a case that’s based on physical or indisputable evidence. I want to see justice served as much as anyone else…but our justice system is based on proof “beyond a reasonable doubt” for a reason. Personal feelings or gut instincts should not be enough for any conviction…because if they are…how can we trust our justice system to both punish the guilty AND protect the innocent? When major cases are built entirely on circumstantial evidence, we tend to see one of two things: either we see an innocent person wrongfully convicted…or we see a guilty criminal walk free. Of course we sometimes get it right…but how confident can we really be that we got it right? Even if we FEEL confident…we still can’t be 100% certain. That’s why circumstantial cases are so controversial. In my friend’s case…a small community got tired of waiting for a decade-long investigation to move forward, and authorities were pressured to move forward with a case that ultimately saw a likely innocent man wrongly convicted. In this case…a major tv show pressured authorities to move forward with a circumstantial case that likely resulted in the acquittal of a killer. Both are examples of the flaws in our justice system.

comments.text:
Agree with you. Nicole likely did it.  But can’t say without a reasonable doubt.  The “drunken confessions” are the biggest point of contention, since there are many.  The “keys” argument falls flat to me… why couldn’t they steal the victim’s keys (maybe they were still there? …that wasn’t revealed in this video)?  It’s not as damning a piece of evidence as it sounds.  Look, I don’t want to get carried away with a defense of Nicole and suggest it’s a random intruder, as there’s no theft… no rape… no motive for a random intruder.  But even if it’s just a marginal possibility (which is why the key argument falling flat is important), that’s important.  All the defense needs is reasonable doubt.  Zero forensic evidence.  

Do I think Nicole did it?  Yes.  Too many witnesses claiming she confessed.  Even her aunt said she admitted to visiting the scene.  

But beyond a reasonable doubt?  Not close.  The key argument is bullshit (unless, again, the victim’s key was found there… not revealed in this video, so I don’t know).  So, all you’re left with is the drunken confessions.  And let’s remember, it’s plausible that BOTH parties are drunk.  Drunken recall after 15 years?  Oh, to be clear, I still believe it.  I think she’s guilty.  But you’re talking about taking someone’s life (life sentence or death).  Over a drunken confession which neither side may be lucid enough to understand?  Again, I think they would be.  Murder will stick in your mind.  But enough to convict someone beyond a reasonable doubt?   Not even close.  

Let me remind folks that we lazily use the wrong terminology in court.  “Not guilty” is not “not guilty”.  It means the evidence is insufficient to convict.  Literally.  That’s not my twisted interpretation.  That’s literally true.  Preponderance of the evidence is 50%.  Beyond a reasonable doubt is what?  I dunno… 70, 80, 90, 95%?   So, if you believe someone is guilty and your confidence is about 60-40, you’d find them not guilty… even though you think they’re guilty.  So, we need better phraseology.  Not guilty does not mean not guilty.  It means not enough evidence to convict.
